author: high
claim: For positive x=BD/DC, y=CE/EA, z=AF/FB, affine coordinates reduce the three cevian incidences to γ=xβ, α=yγ, and β=zα, respectively; hence a common point exists exactly when xyz=1.
evidence: Let a,b,c be the position vectors of the affinely independent vertices A,B,C. Segment division gives D=(b+xc)/(1+x), E=(ya+c)/(1+y), and F=(a+zb)/(1+z). If a point P has unique barycentric coordinates (α,β,γ) with α+β+γ=1, then P lies on AD iff γ=xβ: the coordinates of D are (0,1/(1+x),x/(1+x)), so the affine span of A and D is exactly the set satisfying γ=xβ. The same calculation gives P on BE iff α=yγ and P on CF iff β=zα. If all three hold, none of α,β,γ can vanish (otherwise all do, contradicting their sum 1), and multiplication yields xyz=(γ/β)(α/γ)(β/α)=1. Conversely, if xyz=1, set S=xy+1+x and (α,β,γ)=(xy/S,1/S,x/S); then all three equations hold.

glossary.A: first vertex of the nondegenerate triangle
glossary.B: second vertex of the nondegenerate triangle
glossary.C: third vertex of the nondegenerate triangle
glossary.P: candidate common point of the three cevian lines
